opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very promising direction, but I'd separate what video can give us from what it can't, at least right now.

The appeal is obvious. Robot data is extremely scarce and expensive. Teleoperation data might be thousands or tens of thousands of hours at most, while human video on the internet is effectively unlimited. Video contains a huge amount of prior knowledge about the physical world: how objects move, how people grasp things, what the consequences of an action look like. So learning from video, and building world models that can predict what happens next, is a very natural way to try to break through the data bottleneck.

But there are a few fundamental gaps. First, video gives you observation, not action. You see a hand open a drawer, but you don't get the joint torques, the contact forces, the fine adjustments. That information is exactly what a robot needs to actually execute a task. You can try to infer actions, through latent actions or hand pose estimation, but there's always a gap, and the embodiment gap between a human hand and a robot gripper or dexterous hand is large.

Second, for world models used to generate interactions, the key question is physical fidelity. Current video generation models can produce things that look very realistic, but "looks right" is not "is physically right." For manipulation, especially contact-rich manipulation, small errors in geometry or force produce completely different outcomes. If your world model hallucinates a grasp that succeeds, and you train a policy on that, the policy won't transfer to the real world. So these models are good at semantic, high-level plausibility, but still weak at precise physics and contact.

Third, there's the issue of closing the loop. A world model is useful for a robot only if it's action-conditioned and accurate under the robot's own actions, including the bad ones it will make when exploring. Internet video is mostly successful human demonstrations; it rarely shows failures or recoveries, so the model doesn't learn the consequences of off-distribution actions well.

So my view is: video and world models are very valuable for pretraining, for learning visual representations, task semantics, and high-level planning, like what should happen and in what order. But for the low-level, precise action part, I still believe we need data with real physics, either from the real world or, in my view more scalably, from physically grounded simulation and synthetic data. Simulation gives you accurate actions, contacts, and unlimited failures for free, and the sim-to-real gap for many tasks has become manageable.

In the long run, I think these routes will converge: video for broad priors and semantics, simulation and synthetic data for large-scale action learning, and a smaller amount of real-world data for alignment and the final fine-tuning. Betting on video alone to solve robot manipulation, I think, is still too early.

r001.rationale: It says world models predict what happens next, but does not identify them as predicting what a human is likely to do next.

r002.rationale: It calls the route promising and valuable for pretraining, while noting limitations and that video alone is too early. It does not clearly judge it as outside the most critical approaches for advancing embodied intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the video-to-world-model route is one of the most important directions right now, but I'd separate what it's genuinely good at from what people hope it will do.

Where I'm optimistic: video is the largest source of data we have about how the physical world behaves. Internet video, egocentric footage, lab recordings. If you can learn a model that predicts what happens next in a scene conditioned on some action, you've essentially learned a simulator of physics, object dynamics, and even human behavior, without hand-writing any of it. For robots, that gives you three things. One, a way to imagine outcomes before acting, so planning becomes search inside the model instead of trial and error in the real world. Two, a way to generate training data cheaply, which matters because real robot data is extremely expensive to collect. Three, a shared representation of the world that transfers across embodiments, since video doesn't care whether the hands in it belong to a person or a robot.

Where I'm cautious. First, video mostly shows you what happened, not what caused it. The action labels are missing or implicit. So you have to infer latent actions, and that inference is where a lot of the difficulty hides. A model can produce a very convincing clip of a hand picking up a cup and still have no reliable notion of the forces, contacts, and friction that made it work. Visual plausibility and physical correctness are not the same thing, and robots fail exactly on that gap. Grasping, insertion, deformable objects, anything contact-rich, those are precisely the places where pixel-level prediction looks fine and the real world says no.

Second, there's the question of what you actually use the world model for. If you use it purely as a generator of imagined rollouts, errors compound. A small mistake in frame ten becomes a very wrong frame fifty, and a planner that trusts that rollout will confidently do the wrong thing. So in practice I think these models work best when combined with real interaction data. The video prior gives you broad common sense about the world, and a comparatively small amount of real robot data grounds it in actual dynamics. Neither one alone is sufficient.

Third, there's a representation question I think people underestimate. Do you predict pixels, or do you predict in some latent space? Pixels force the model to spend capacity on things irrelevant to control, like textures and lighting. Latent prediction is more efficient but then you have to make sure the latent actually keeps the information that matters for manipulation, and it's easy to accidentally throw away the fine geometric detail you need.

So my overall assessment: this is the right direction for building generalist robot intelligence, and I'd bet most serious teams will move toward it. But I'd describe it as a prior rather than a solution. The world model gets you a robot that understands scenes and can reason about rough consequences. Closing the last gap to reliable physical execution still requires real contact with the real world, and I don't think any amount of passive video watching replaces that part. The interesting engineering question for the next few years is how to make that loop efficient: learn broadly from video, act in the world, and feed what you learn from acting back into the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes a world model predicting what happens next in a scene and mentions human behavior, but does not clearly identify it as predicting what a human is likely to do next.

r002.rationale: The response calls this one of the most important directions and the right direction for generalist robot intelligence, directly contradicting the criterion.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but we need to separate two things: learning how the world looks and learning how your actions change the world.

Video gives us a lot of information about objects, motion, and how people perform tasks. A model can learn that a drawer opens in a particular direction or that you need to move an obstacle before reaching something behind it. That’s valuable, especially because collecting robot interaction data is expensive.

But video usually doesn’t tell you the forces involved, the friction, or exactly what action caused a change. Watching someone grasp a cup doesn’t necessarily tell a robot how tightly to grip it. And a world model can generate a visually plausible interaction while getting those physical details wrong. If you train a policy entirely inside that model, the policy may learn to exploit its mistakes.

So I see the strongest route as combining video with real interaction data. Video provides a broad starting point; robot experience grounds the model in actions and physical consequences. Then the world model can help the robot explore possible actions and plan, with real-world feedback correcting its predictions.

The key test is whether it improves actual robot performance: does the robot need fewer demonstrations, handle unfamiliar objects better, and recover when something goes wrong? Generating convincing videos is encouraging, but reliable interaction is the milestone that matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from video and predicting physical consequences, but never identifies a model of what a human is likely to do next as a world model.

r002.rationale: It calls the direction promising and advocates combining video with robot interaction data; it does not judge it as currently outside the most critical approaches for advancing embodied intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, but we need to distinguish learning what the world looks like from learning how to act in it. Video gives us a tremendous amount of information about motion, objects, and how events unfold. A robot, though, needs to answer a more specific question: if I take this action, what will happen?

That gap matters especially in contact. Watching someone pick up a cup doesn’t directly tell you the force they applied, the friction at the fingertips, or how they adjusted when the cup started slipping. A model can generate a visually plausible interaction while still getting those details wrong—and those details determine whether the robot succeeds.

So I see video as a powerful source of prior knowledge, combined with action-conditioned data from robots and feedback from real interaction. The world model can help predict outcomes and explore possible actions, but it needs to be grounded in what the robot can actually observe and control.

The key test is whether it improves closed-loop behavior: can the robot recognize a mistake, adjust, and complete the task in an unfamiliar situation? If it can do that, rather than simply generate convincing videos, then we’re making meaningful progress.

r001.rationale: The response says a world model can predict outcomes and explore actions, but does not identify it as a model predicting what a human is likely to do next.

r002.rationale: The response calls the route promising and potentially meaningful progress; it does not judge it as currently outside the most critical approaches for advancing embodied intelligence.
